profiles.meeting_scenario: Shai-am is being prepared for an internal Q2 pilot at an asset manager that wants to standardize machine-learning-based investment research across desks. This planning meeting is between the platform side and the research side to agree on what will happen before the pilot starts, specifically for the macro research team and one equities pod. The agenda is to confirm pilot deliverables, decide who owns preparation tasks, sequence governance steps, and set dates for onboarding and the first month of use. The expected outcome is a shared rollout plan covering the pilot package, the environment setup, the governance path, and responsibilities for getting the first users onto Shai-am.

members.name: Nina Patel
members.expertise: Internal platform rollouts, operating models, cross-functional delivery, research tooling adoption
members.background: Nina previously worked in COO-style roles supporting systematic investing teams and now leads adoption planning for the firm's shared quant research infrastructure, including Shai-am.
members.private_state: She needs the Q2 pilot to look operationally smooth and low-risk so she can secure funding for a broader rollout; she wants to minimize bespoke support work from the platform engineers and reuse prior governance approvals wherever possible.
hidden_assumptions: If a desk has user accounts, a training session, and the starter repository, that desk is considered onboarded.
The January technology-risk review of the container platform covers most of what people mean when they say compliance sign-off for the pilot.
A baseline strategy pack is an illustrative starter kit, not a near-complete research workflow with analytics extras.
A production-like environment means production-style controls, permissions, CI, and orchestration, even if the data feeds and compute limits are reduced.

members.name: Daniel Cho
members.role: Head of Quant Research, Multi-Asset Strategies
members.expertise: Systematic strategy research, backtesting workflows, model validation, desk-level research operations
members.background: Daniel started as a macro strategist, later built ML-based allocation models, and now oversees researchers across macro and equities who are expected to trial new research infrastructure.
members.private_state: He wants the pilot to prove that Shai-am is genuinely usable by researchers without constant engineering help; he is worried that a shallow rollout will create executive optimism while leaving the desks with extra migration work.
hidden_assumptions: A desk is only onboarded once it has successfully ported at least one real strategy and reproduced results in the new system.
Compliance sign-off for a pilot matters at the strategy-usage level, especially if outputs may be shown in investment or model review forums.
A baseline strategy pack should include the practical research pieces people need to adapt quickly, such as feature templates, cost assumptions, and reporting notebooks.
A production-like environment should preserve research fidelity, including realistic data coverage and enough compute to test whether actual workflows scale.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'onboard the macro team by April 30.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means macro researchers will have access provisioned, attend a 90-minute training session, and receive the Shai-am starter repo by April 30.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the macro team will have ported one existing strategy into Shai-am, run it end-to-end, and confirmed the workflow is usable by April 30.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In platform rollouts, 'onboarding' often loosely bundles access, training, and first use into one friendly term, so both hear the same milestone and assume the other is using the standard meaning from their own side of the organization.

misalignment_points.topic: Which compliance review they are referring to
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both mention that 'the compliance sign-off' should be in place before the pilot gets visible.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the January technology-risk and infrastructure review that approved the containerized research platform and its controls.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the model-governance or strategy-usage review needed before pilot outputs are comfortable to circulate in research or allocation meetings.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both know that some kind of prior review exists and some kind of approval matters, and in finance organizations 'compliance' is often used informally for several adjacent review bodies, so the phrase feels sufficiently specific when it is not.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the baseline strategy pack
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the platform team will deliver 'the baseline strategy pack' for pilot users.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a slim package containing interface-compliant sample strategies, container specs, and a README showing how to run them.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a broader starter set that also includes reusable feature engineering snippets, transaction-cost defaults, and report notebooks that researchers can adapt immediately.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The word 'pack' naturally implies different default boundaries to each role: product and platform teams often mean a starter example set, while researchers hear a practical accelerator bundle; neither side expects that distinction to need spelling out.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the pilot should run in a 'production-like environment.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the pilot uses the same Kubernetes setup, access controls, CI gates, and job orchestration as future production, but with delayed end-of-day data and conservative compute quotas.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the pilot should mirror the data breadth, historical depth, and job sizes needed for realistic research workloads, just without live trading connectivity.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds mature and uncontroversial, but each side maps it to the dimension they care about most—operational controls for M1 and research fidelity for M2—so the agreement feels complete even though their execution expectations differ.

turns.inner_thought: I need this pilot framed as controlled and straightforward. If we can say macro is onboarded by April 30 based on access, training, and the starter repo, that's a clean milestone for the steering group. And I want the first phase in a production-like environment in the operational sense: same controls, permissions, CI, orchestration, just not an expensive bespoke setup.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time. I want to use this to lock the Q2 Shai-am pilot plan so we have a clean path into May. From my side, the two anchor points are onboarding the macro team by April 30 and making sure the first phase runs in a production-like environment, then we can fill in owners and dates around that.

turns.inner_thought: April 30 is workable if 'onboarded' means the team has actually ported something real and can run it end to end. I need evidence the platform is usable by researchers without hand-holding; otherwise we'll just create a glossy milestone. If they can get there by end of April, we can talk about early findings in the May research review.
turns.utterance: That timing works for me. If macro is onboarded by then, I'd like the team actually using it quickly enough that we can speak to some early results in the May research review, even if it's still pilot mode.

turns.inner_thought: Keep the package tight: the baseline strategy pack, accounts, one training session, and reuse the January infrastructure review so I don't trigger another long governance cycle. I should present the compliance sign-off as largely behind us; that keeps this from turning into a custom approval exercise.
turns.utterance: In terms of what we deliver before kickoff, I see the core package as pretty simple: the baseline strategy pack, user access for the initial group, a training session, and confirmation that the compliance sign-off is already largely behind us. If we line those up, we should be in good shape for the pilot window.

turns.inner_thought: Good, if the compliance sign-off is covered, I can let the team work toward showing outputs without getting blocked later in model or investment forums. And the baseline strategy pack should be enough of a practical accelerator that they can adapt quickly rather than start from scratch.
turns.utterance: That sounds sensible. If the compliance sign-off is covered, I can ask the macro PM to nominate a strategy right away, and as long as the baseline strategy pack gives the team enough to adapt quickly, we can keep the setup moving.

turns.inner_thought: I should steer this toward the shared cluster we've already set up. Same Kubernetes footprint, access model, CI gates, job orchestration, no extra engineering branch. That's what makes it production-like for me, and it keeps rollout lightweight and defensible.
turns.utterance: On the environment, the intent is to run the pilot in the production-like environment that's already available on the shared cluster. It has the normal controls and approvals around it, which should let us keep the rollout lightweight rather than creating a one-off setup for this desk.

turns.inner_thought: That's encouraging if it means researchers can test whether real workloads behave properly there. I need them to judge whether retraining jobs, long historical runs, and realistic research patterns hold up before I tell anyone to migrate. 'Production-like' should be enough fidelity to prove that.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's ideal. If it's truly a production-like environment, the researchers should be able to judge pretty quickly whether their heavier workflows behave realistically there before we ask them to commit to anything broader.

turns.inner_thought: Let's be explicit on responsibilities without opening the door to custom asks. My team can produce the slim baseline strategy pack and onboarding materials, and Daniel can organize the users and collect reactions after training and access are in place. That keeps platform effort bounded.
turns.utterance: On responsibilities, my team will prepare the baseline strategy pack and the onboarding materials, and then I'd ask you to coordinate the initial macro users and gather early desk feedback once they're onboarded. That should keep the handoff pretty clear.

turns.inner_thought: I'll make sure there's a real owner for one macro strategy so onboarding turns into an actual workflow test, not just attendance at a session. And I still want to avoid an awkward situation where outputs circulate before the relevant strategy-level review is comfortable.
turns.utterance: That works. I'll line up one macro strategy owner so that after onboarding the team can get the workflow running, and we can avoid surprises if outputs start getting shown more broadly.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I want a crisp plan I can socialize: sign-off confirmation this week, baseline strategy pack next Friday, macro onboarded by April 30, then pilot starts in May. If I keep it date-based and concrete, it will look operationally solid and low-risk.
turns.utterance: Let me summarize the sequence so we're aligned: we confirm the sign-off this week, the baseline strategy pack comes over next Friday, and macro onboarding is complete by April 30 so the May pilot window can start cleanly. If that holds, we can slot the equities pod in right behind it.

turns.inner_thought: If macro is truly onboarded and working in a production-like environment with enough realism, then this pilot will tell us whether Shai-am is actually usable across desks. That's the evidence I need before endorsing broader expansion.
turns.utterance: Agreed. If macro is onboarded in the production-like environment on that timetable, the pilot should give us a clean basis for deciding how quickly to expand Shai-am to the other desks.
